items.description: arXiv:2611.31301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. items.description: arXiv:2611.31427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents operate through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, feedback loops, and resource constraints. items.description: arXiv:2611.31570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In playtesting games, a human operator is typically required to test most gameplay elements. items.description: arXiv:2611.31762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We refactor existing Lean 4 proofs to reduce source length and checking cost while preserving theorem statements and compatibility across Lean versions. items.description: arXiv:2611.32138v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In embedding-based video anomaly detection (VAD), normal clips can have high similarity to anomalous descriptions, an anomaly bias that leads to false positives. items.description: arXiv:2611.32148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A learned critic can improve a pretrained flow-matching policy by steering sampled actions toward higher predicted value. However, even a critic that fits the behavior data well can provide misleading action gradients. Gradient components pointing away from the data-supported region are weakly constrained by behavior data and can lead guidance to exploit critic extrapolation errors. We introduce RetraQ (Retraction-based Q-guidance), which uses geometry encoded by the pretrained flow to constrain both the direction and the destination of critic guidance. A single velocity evaluation of the frozen flow defines a denoising map. RetraQ filters the critic gradient with the map's Jacobian and applies the map itself to correct the updated action.

items.description: arXiv:2611.32233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time is a fundamental dimension of robotic intelligence: a robot may fail despite physically correct actions if it acts outside a valid time window, responds too slowly to an event, or fails to meet required throughput. items.description: arXiv:2611.32483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. items.description: arXiv:2611.32496v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. items.description: arXiv:2611.32529v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learned driving planners keep being updated after deployment as new logs arrive, yet continual learning evaluations rarely ask whether an update improves on the deployed model, and their verdicts rest on unstated evaluation choices. items.description: arXiv:2611.32533v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. items.description: arXiv:2611.32623v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reference-based MT evaluation assumes the human reference is correct and better than the systems it scores. items.description: arXiv:2611.32642v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dynamic obstacle avoidance is essential for safely deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments, where rapidly approaching objects require immediate evasive responses. items.description: arXiv:2611.32649v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. items.description: arXiv:2611.32803v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. items.description: arXiv:2611.32820v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. items.title: On Potentiality and Actuality Of Foundation Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.32991v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation models are built through large-scale pretraining, often followed by post-training, and are then adapted to specific tasks and behaviors. But, does the adaptation add truly new capabilities, or the base model already holds it? We decompose the update induced by different adaptations into a component shared across all inputs and a residual that varies with the input. We find that the shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that learns a constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. items.title: One, No One and One Hundred Thousand CTs: Testing Anatomical Control in Text-to-CT Generation
items.description: arXiv:2611.33003v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in deep learning and the public availability of computed tomography (CT) datasets with paired reports have enabled many Text-to-CT generators. However, their evaluations almost always differ in preprocessing and metrics, which hinders comparison. Moreover, their protocols almost never test how editing the report changes the CT, not even at the same seed, so the report is often assumed to control the anatomy without evidence of how much and how consistently it does. items.title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
items.description: arXiv:2611.33004v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. items.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies
items.description: arXiv:2611.33010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. items.title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
items.description: arXiv:2611.33031v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly.
